prime.problem: Listing every way to split $20k across 4 options means checking 194,481 tuples to find 220. The product rule doesn't fit either: the units are identical, so assigning them one by one counts the same split many times.
prime.fits: The second counting card. Inclusion–exclusion corrected overlaps after the fact; this card avoids them with a one-to-one match between splits and bar positions, and brings inclusion–exclusion back only for upper caps.
expect: a case split for 'at least 3 of 4'
prime.goal: Turn a distribution problem into a choice of bar positions, handle minimums and caps, and say when the splits are not equally likely.

attend: Why is every split exactly one arrangement of 9 stars and 3 bars, and what do two bars side by side mean?
How does paying the minimums first turn x<sub>i</sub> ≥ m<sub>i</sub> into a problem with no constraints?
Why do the five cases of 'at least three of four' not overlap, so you can simply add them?
Which assumption breaks if the units are 20 named employees rather than identical dollars?
Why are the 220 strategies not equally likely if each $1k unit picks its opportunity at random?

must: Units identical, bins labelled → a split is just a row of stars and bars → choose which k − 1 of the n + k − 1 slots hold bars → C(n + k − 1, k − 1)
Minimum m<sub>i</sub> per bin → substitute x<sub>i</sub> = m<sub>i</sub> + y<sub>i</sub> → only n − Σm stars are left → C(12, 3) = 220, against the 1,771 you get by splitting all 20 freely
An upper cap can't be paid in advance → count the overflows (give one bin cap + 1 first) and subtract them with inclusion–exclusion → 220 − 75 = 145 with an $8k cap
Stars and bars counts outcomes, not probabilities → when units choose bins at random, each split is weighted by its multinomial coefficient → 20-0-0-0 arises one way, 5-5-5-5 arises 20!/(5!)⁴ ways
elevated: 'At least r of k bins used' → one stars-and-bars count per set of used bins, each with its own minimums → 5 terms here, but the count of subsets grows like 2<sup>k</sup>

compress.prompt: From memory, draw one star-and-bar row for a strategy of your choice, and explain in 3 sentences why the count is C(12, 3). Then write the one-line case sum for part 2.
checklist: n identical units, k labelled bins, k − 1 bars
a split corresponds to exactly one choice of bar slots
part 2 is a sum over which bins are used: 220 + 78 + 78 + 91 + 105 = 572
splits are outcomes; random units make them unequally likely

retrieve.q: Explain why stars and bars needs identical units but labelled bins. What changes if either assumption flips?
answer: identical units: only how many land in each bin matters, so a split is a star/bar row
distinct units: each unit picks a bin, 4<sup>20</sup> ways
identical bins: you are counting integer partitions, which have no closed form like this

retrieve.q: Walk through the 'skip #3' case of part 2: which minimums are paid, how many stars and bars remain, and what count results?
Every option is capped at $8k. Compare a DP table with stars and bars plus inclusion–exclusion: what does each cost, and when would you switch?
answer: stars and bars with I–E: subtract the strategies where some bin overflows, 220 − (10 + 10 + 20 + 35) = 145
DP over ways[bin][amount]: O(k·n²) steps, also 145
switch to the DP when the rules are irregular (a different cap and exceptions per bin) and the I–E terms get messy

compare.q: Inclusion–exclusion corrects an overcount afterwards; stars and bars builds a one-to-one match so there is nothing to correct. Which design choice avoids the overlap here, and where does this card still need the correction?
answer: the match between a split and its bar positions counts each split once by construction
lower limits are absorbed by the substitution x<sub>i</sub> = m<sub>i</sub> + y<sub>i</sub>
upper caps can't be absorbed, so the overflows are subtracted with I–E

compare.q: The closed form against a DP over (bins used, amount so far): what does each show, and when does the DP win?
answer: DP: ways(k, n) = Σ ways(k − 1, n − x) over the allowed x, so it handles any per-bin rule
closed form: O(1) arithmetic, and it shows the structure (slots and bars)
the DP wins with irregular constraints; the closed form wins on paper and in an exam

predict.q: Now each of the 20 $1k units picks one of the 4 opportunities uniformly at random, with no minimums. Which split is more likely, 20-0-0-0 or 5-5-5-5, and by roughly how much? Commit first.
predict.answer: 5-5-5-5, by a factor of 20!/(5!)⁴ = 11,732,745,024, about 1.2 × 10<sup>10</sup>. Stars and bars counts each split once, but with random units a split's probability is its multinomial coefficient ÷ 4<sup>20</sup>. The split 20-0-0-0 has one arrangement; 5-5-5-5 has 20!/(5!)⁴.

apply.task: The investor now has $25k, with the same minimums (2, 2, 3, 4). Recompute part 1 and part 2 by hand, writing the stars, bars and C(·, ·) for each of the 5 cases. Then run at_least(25, mins, 3) to check.
apply.done: Part 1 is C(17, 3) = 680. Part 2 is 680 + 2·C(18, 2) + C(19, 2) + C(20, 2) = 680 + 306 + 171 + 190 = 1,347. Both match the code and a brute force over all 26⁴ tuples.
apply.hint: Each extra $1k adds one star to every case: the all-four case goes from 9 to 14 stars.

Which relationship is still fuzzy: split → bar positions, or cap → inclusion–exclusion?
Would you have summed the five cases, or tried one formula for 'at least 3'? Why does the case split work?
What will you revisit before the bridge-hands card?
